paragraphs.heading: Velocity from a viewpoint
paragraphs.text: Relative velocity is the velocity of an object B as measured in the rest frame of an observer A, the frame in which A stays still. It is written v _(B∣A). Its size is called the relative speed. You can also say "the velocity of B with respect to A", or speak of the coordinate system where A is always at rest.

paragraphs.heading: The everyday case
paragraphs.text: When all speeds are far below the speed of light, the classical, or Newtonian, picture works well. This limit goes with what is called the Galilean transformation.

paragraphs.heading: A walk on a train
paragraphs.text: Picture a man on top of a train, at its back edge. At 1:00 pm he starts walking forward at 10 km/h while the train moves at 40 km/h. One hour later, at 2:00 pm, he is 50 km from where he began, which by definition means 50 km/h. So in the classical picture, working out a relative velocity like this simply means adding the two velocities together: his walking speed plus the speed of the train.

paragraphs.heading: Chaining viewpoints
paragraphs.text: The difference between two position vectors, r _B − r _A, gives where B sits as seen from A. Velocities chain in a similar way through a third observer, C. The velocity of B as seen by C equals the velocity of B as seen by A, plus the velocity of A as seen by C. Written this way, the rule has a tidy symmetry that makes it easy to learn and remember.

paragraphs.heading: Where simple adding fails
paragraphs.text: This classical rule clashes with special relativity. It wrongly predicts that different observers would measure different speeds for light. The relativistic formula shows an odd lack of symmetry, linked to Thomas precession and to the fact that two Lorentz transformations in a row rotate the coordinate system. That rotation leaves a vector's size unchanged, so the relative speed is still symmetrical. For two objects moving in parallel directions, the relativistic formula looks much like the one for adding relativistic velocities.
